search_stop.justification: Every federal census in which Elizabeth appears (1850 original image plus index, 1860, 1870, 1880) was examined, and so were her daughters' censuses that give a mother's birthplace (Sarah Martha 1880; Amanda 1880 original, 1900, 1910). A FAN survey covered the 1850 Turnbow households, and the church record attached in the tree, the Mississippi death-certificate index and the Find a Grave index were checked. Alabama did not require birth registration until 1908, so the census testimony is the main evidence that exists for a woman born in 1823. The question is answered at state level (Alabama). The county is not named in any record and would need a separate question.

stop_criteria.conflict_resolution: c_001 is resolved in favor of Alabama. England is explained as a derivative transcription error, and Mississippi as a daughter's second-hand answer.

stop_criteria.independent_verification: Four separate enumerations of her own household (1850-1880) plus her daughter Sarah Martha in a separate household. These share a family informant pool but are distinct recordings by different enumerators.
stop_criteria.original_substitution: The decisive 1850 entry and the 1880 Ainsworth line were verified on original images. The 1860, 1870 and 1880 Barker entries remain index-only but are consistent with each other.
stop_criteria.overturn_risk: Low for the state. An obituary, a Bible record or a true LDS membership register could name a county, but none is likely to move her birth out of Alabama given five concordant statements and the Turnbow siblings' Alabama births.
stop_criteria.repository_breadth: Federal censuses 1850-1910, the Mississippi death-certificate index, Find a Grave index, the LDS district minutes and Turnbow FAN censuses were searched on FamilySearch. No vital birth records exist for Alabama in 1823.

output.text_response:
Here's a strategic plan for browsing unindexed image volumes in the Flynn research, based on the current project state.

---

## Unindexed Browse Strategy — Flynn Research

**Where research stands:** Thomas Flynn is identified as Patrick's father through two sources — the 1860 census (Patrick, age 15, in Thomas's Schuylkill County household) and the 1908 death certificate (names Thomas as father, but the informant was a son-in-law, making it secondary). Patrick's **mother remains unidentified**, and the in-progress plan item targeting Thomas Flynn's probate file is the current open thread.

---

### Priority 1 — Schuylkill County Probate Files, 1870–1890 *(already in your plan, finish this first)*

This is the most direct corroboration available. Thomas Flynn's estate papers, if found, would likely enumerate all heirs — naming Patrick as a son and possibly revealing the mother's name or death date. FamilySearch holds Pennsylvania probate records, but the estate file packets (inventories, distributions, bonds) are typically unindexed image volumes. Browse the Schuylkill County Orphans' Court dockets and the accompanying file images for Thomas Flynn entries in the 1870–1895 window.

---

### Priority 2 — Catholic Parish Registers, Schuylkill County Mining Communities

The Schuylkill County coal region had a large Irish Catholic immigrant population. Patrick's baptismal record and the marriage record of Thomas Flynn would **name the mother directly**. These registers are digitized on FamilySearch but are overwhelmingly unindexed. Browse in this order:
- **St. Patrick's, Pottsville** (oldest Irish parish; baptisms from the 1840s)
- **St. Vincent de Paul, Minersville**
- **Annunciation or St. Mary's parishes in Shenandoah and Mahanoy City** (if the family moved within the region)

A baptismal entry for Patrick around 1844–1846 would name both parents. A marriage entry for Thomas Flynn would give the mother's maiden name and marriage year.

---

### Priority 3 — Schuylkill County Naturalization Records (Court of Common Pleas)

If Thomas Flynn immigrated from Ireland (probable given the region and era), his declaration of intention and petition for naturalization are in the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas. FamilySearch has digitized these but many are unindexed. These records often include the applicant's age, country of birth, and sometimes the specific county of origin — which could open Irish civil or church records downstream. Browse the naturalization dockets and stub volumes for the 1850–1875 period.

---

### Priority 4 — 1850 Federal Census (Schuylkill County, if not yet checked)

The 1850 census is indexed on FamilySearch, but **if a name-search already failed**, a page-by-page browse of the Schuylkill County enumeration districts where Thomas might have lived is worth doing. At this census Patrick would be about five years old; his mother would be enumerated by name in the household. Township-level browsing is feasible since Schuylkill County enumerations are organized by township.

---

### Priority 5 — Pennsylvania Vital Records Volumes, Pre-1906

Pennsylvania had no mandatory statewide vital registration before 1906, but some county-level and church-based birth/death registers survive. Schuylkill County has a few surviving local civil registers from the 1870s–1890s that are unindexed on FamilySearch. These are thin, but a death entry for Thomas Flynn or his wife could surface quickly.

---

### Suggested Sequence

| Order | Record Set | What you're looking for |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Schuylkill Co. probate files, 1870–1895 | Thomas Flynn's estate — names heirs/children |
| 2 | Catholic baptismal registers, Pottsville & Minersville | Patrick's baptism (names both parents); Thomas's marriage (names wife) |
| 3 | Schuylkill Co. naturalization dockets, 1850–1875 | Thomas Flynn's declaration — age, Irish county of origin |
| 4 | 1850 census page-browse, Schuylkill Co. | Mother's name in the Flynn household |
| 5 | County vital registers, 1870s–1890s | Thomas or wife's death — may name survivors |

The **probate file** and **Catholic parish registers** are the highest-yield targets because both have a realistic chance of naming the mother — which is the single biggest gap left in this case.

Vital events are recorded in parish church books (kirkeboeger); baptism entries name both parents. Civil registration is much later.
The Stagstrup parish register is only ~3% name-indexed on FamilySearch — plan to browse the register images by year rather than rely on the index.

items.rationale: The 1850 Jasper residence comes from an unsourced tree and may be wrong, or the household may sit just across a county line (he is in neighboring Smith County by 1860). Widen the 1850 search to all adjoining counties and to statewide Mississippi with an England birthplace filter.

Ancestry's 1850 census index is an independent transcription; a name FamilySearch's index garbled may be readable there. Index searching is free; image viewing needs a subscription or a FamilySearch Center/library visit.

Jasper County tax rolls 1834-1896 survive as browse-only images in 'Mississippi, State Archives, Various Records, 1818-1952' (collection 1919687). Annual rolls place Jonathan Barker in the county around 1850, corroborate the census entry, and can narrow when he arrived. Most Jasper courthouse records start only in 1904-1906, so tax rolls are one of the few local sources left for this period.

The 1845 Mississippi state census returns for Jasper County (browse-only images in collection 1919687) list heads of household with tallies of household members. A Jonathan Barker entry would corroborate residence before 1850 and the size of his household.

Bridge record to confirm identity: the 1860 Smith County household (claimed on the tree) should list the same wife and the older children seen in 1850, with ages advanced 10 years.
